Delilah
dē-lī'lä
n. (the woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved, who sold the secret of his strength to the lords of the Philistines)
From Hebrew Delilah, most naturally taken from dalal, to be weak, brought low, to languish — hence she that weakened or the feeble one. The narrative uses the cognate idea at the crisis: his strength went from him, and he became weak as another man.

Biblical Definition

Delilah is the last of the three Philistine women in Samson's life and the only one Scripture says he loved: “he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah” (Jdg 16:4). The lords of the Philistines bought her outright, eleven hundred pieces of silver from each of five cities, and her question was never disguised: “Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee” (Jdg 16:6). Three times he lied, three times she bound him and cried that the Philistines were upon him, and three times he woke and broke the bonds — and stayed. The narrative is merciless about the mechanism: “when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death” (Jdg 16:16), and he told her all his heart. Then “she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him” (Jdg 16:19). The dreadful sentence is that he awoke and did not know “that the LORD was departed from him” (Jdg 16:20). The Philistines took him, put out his eyes, bound him with fetters of brass, and set him grinding in the prison house (Jdg 16:21). Delilah collects her silver and leaves the story; Scripture never mentions her again.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Delilah; in sacred history she is the woman of the valley of Sorek who betrayed Samson to the lords of the Philistines.

expand to see more

DELILAH, n. A proper name; a woman of the valley of Sorek, beloved by Samson.

The lords of the Philistines hired her with eleven hundred pieces of silver apiece.

Thrice he deceived her concerning the secret of his strength, and thrice she bound him.

She pressed him daily with her words until his soul was vexed unto death, and he told her all his heart.

She caused the seven locks of his head to be shaven, and delivered him to his enemies.

Key Scripture

Jdg 16:4 — "And it came to pass afterward, that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah."

Jdg 16:16 — "And it came to pass, when she pressed him daily with her words, and urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death;"

Jdg 16:19 — "And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him."

Jdg 16:20 — "And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him."

Modern Corruption

Delilah is now regularly rehabilitated as a woman of an occupied people acting rationally under pressure, and Samson recast as her abuser. The text presents a bought betrayer and a Nazarite who threw away his vow, and it holds each of them responsible.

expand to see more

The revisionist reading is by now the standard one in popular retellings: Delilah was a Philistine under a foreign strongman's attentions, with no power and no options, and the money was survival rather than greed; the real culprit is Samson, and the older reading of the passage is merely the suspicion of women dressed up as exegesis. Judges gives no support to any of it. The silver is offered before she acts and she does not decline it; she asks her question openly, four times, after three demonstrations that the answer will be used to bind him; she summons the barber; she cries the Philistines be upon thee while the ambush waits in the chamber. The text does not describe a cornered woman. It describes a paid one.

Nor does Scripture spare Samson, and this is why the chapter is not a tract against women but against a particular folly. He was a Nazarite from the womb who had already given away every part of the vow but the hair — he had touched the dead lion, drunk at a feast, and gone repeatedly to Philistine women — and the shaving was the last item on a long inventory of contempt. Proverbs describes the pattern exactly: “With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him” (Pro 7:21), and warns the young man to keep his way far from her door. The horror of Judges 16 is not the shears; it is the sentence, he wist not that the LORD was departed from him. A man may lose the presence of God by inches and be the last to notice.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Delilah (H1807), Delilah; dalal (H1809), to be weak, brought low; Soreq (H7796), Sorek, the valley of her dwelling; nazir (H5139), Nazarite, one separated; machlaphah (H4253), lock or plait of hair.

expand to see more

Hebrew Delilah (H1807) — Delilah; the woman of the valley of Sorek.

Hebrew dalal (H1809) — to be brought low, to languish; the likely root of her name.

Hebrew Soreq (H7796) — Sorek; the valley on the Philistine border.

Hebrew nazir (H5139) — Nazarite; the separated state Samson forfeited.

Hebrew machlaphah (H4253) — lock of hair; the seven locks shaved away.

Usage

"“He loved a woman in the valley of Sorek” — the affection that cost a judge his eyes."

"“She pressed him daily with her words” — betrayal by attrition, not by ambush."

"“He wist not that the LORD was departed from him” — the worst sentence in the book of Judges."
